questions.stem: In the post-maturity stage of the business life cycle, the three possible outcomes are:
options: profit, liquidity and solvency
steady state, decline and renewal
seed, start-up and early-stage growth
growth, expansion and maturity
questions.explanation: After maturity a business may hold its position (steady state), lose sales and profit (decline) or transform itself (renewal). Seed, start-up and growth are earlier stages of the life cycle.

questions.stem: A Brisbane department store's sales and profit have barely changed for six years: it holds its customers but is not growing. Which post-maturity outcome does this describe?
options: decline
renewal
early growth
steady state
questions.explanation: Stable sales and profit with no growth is a steady state. Decline would show falling sales and profit, and renewal would show the business transforming itself to grow again.

questions.stem: Which is a typical challenge of the post-maturity stage?
options: hiring enough staff to keep up with very rapid sales growth
customers move to newer products and rivals as the market changes
finding its first customers for a product that has never been sold
raising seed capital from family and friends to test an idea
questions.explanation: In post-maturity, changing technology, tastes and competition draw customers away from established products. Finding first customers, raising seed capital and rapid hiring are seed, start-up and growth challenges.

questions.stem: A Queensland newspaper's print sales have fallen for ten years, advertisers have moved online and losses are growing. If it takes no action, the most likely outcome is:
options: a return to the growth stage once advertisers come back to print media
continued decline, which may end in the business having to exit the market
a steady state, because established businesses are always protected from change
automatic renewal, as falling sales always lead businesses to innovate
questions.explanation: Ongoing falls in sales and growing losses describe decline, and without repositioning or renewal this can end in sale, closure or administration. Nothing in the data suggests advertisers will return or that renewal happens on its own.

questions.stem: Rebranding is when a business:
options: buys a competitor at the same stage of production
changes its name, logo, slogan or visual identity
changes the target market and how customers see it
sells its assets and closes the business for good
questions.explanation: Rebranding changes the business's visible identity, such as its name or logo. Changing the target market and the customer's perception of the business is repositioning.

questions.stem: A tired budget motel chain renovates its rooms, raises its prices and targets business travellers who want comfort and fast wi-fi. This is best described as:
options: horizontal growth, buying another motel chain to increase market share
repositioning, changing the target market and customers' perception
rebranding, changing only the chain's name and its visual identity
voluntary administration, handing control to an independent person
questions.explanation: Repositioning changes what the business offers and to whom, so customers see it differently. Rebranding alone would change its look without changing the product or the target market.

questions.stem: A business in decline replaces its logo and colours but keeps the same outdated products, prices and service. Sales keep falling. What is the most valid explanation?
options: the business should have entered voluntary administration before rebranding
a rebrand changes appearance, but customers' reasons for leaving remain
the new logo was not used for long enough to change customer behaviour
rebranding always reduces sales, so it should never be attempted at all
questions.explanation: Rebranding alone does not address why customers left, such as outdated products; repositioning changes the offering itself. Rebranding can help when combined with real changes, so it is not always harmful.

questions.stem: Under voluntary administration, a company's directors:
options: appoint an independent administrator to take control of the company
continue to run the company with no outside person involved in it at all
are ordered by a court to sell the company's assets to its staff
transfer ownership of the company directly to its largest customer
questions.explanation: In voluntary administration the directors appoint an independent administrator, who takes control and investigates the company's future. It usually happens when directors believe the company is, or soon will be, insolvent.

questions.stem: After investigating a company in voluntary administration, the administrator reports to creditors, who then decide its future. Which is one of the possible outcomes?
options: the government takes over the company and pays all of its debts in full
a deed of company arrangement setting out how debts will be dealt with
the creditors take personal ownership of the directors' private homes
the company is automatically listed on the stock exchange to raise funds
questions.explanation: Creditors can vote to return the company to the directors, to accept a deed of company arrangement, or to put the company into liquidation. The other outcomes are not options in voluntary administration.

questions.stem: A supplier owed a large sum by a struggling Ipswich company applies to the court, which orders the company to be wound up and appoints a liquidator. This exit is:
options: voluntary, because the directors chose to hand the company to a liquidator
a merger, because the supplier combines with the company to form one firm
a rebrand, because the company changes its name to avoid its creditors
involuntary, because it is started by a creditor rather than the owners
questions.explanation: When creditors force a company into administration or liquidation through the court, the exit is involuntary. In a voluntary process, the directors or owners start it themselves.

questions.stem: In liquidation, a liquidator:
options: advises the directors on a new marketing campaign to lift sales
lends the company money so it can keep trading for another year
sells the company's assets and distributes the proceeds to creditors
takes over the company to return it to growth for its own shareholders
questions.explanation: Liquidation ends the company: the liquidator converts its assets to cash and pays creditors in the order the law sets. It is an exit, not a plan to keep trading.

questions.stem: The owner of a declining but still profitable Toowoomba bakery wants to retire. Which exit option is most likely to give her the best return?
options: selling the business as a going concern while it is still profitable
waiting until it makes losses and then entering voluntary administration
closing it immediately and selling the ovens separately for scrap value
allowing creditors to apply to the court to have the business wound up
questions.explanation: A profitable business can be sold as a going concern, so the buyer pays for its customers, reputation and assets together. Waiting for losses or forced liquidation would reduce the value, and scrapping assets loses the goodwill.

questions.stem: An acquisition (takeover) occurs when:
options: a business divides itself into two separately owned companies
one business buys a controlling interest in another business
two businesses agree to share their advertising for one season
a business sells its products in another country through an agent
questions.explanation: In an acquisition one business gains control of another by buying a controlling interest. In a merger, two businesses combine by agreement to form a single business.

questions.stem: Two declining regional radio networks merge to share studios, staff and advertising sales. How might this help them reposition?
options: combined resources cut costs and give a larger audience to offer advertisers
the merger removes any need to follow listener tastes or new technology
merging guarantees that both networks will return to the growth stage at once
the merged business can ignore competition law, as it is now much larger
questions.explanation: Merging can achieve economies of scale and a bigger audience, which strengthens the combined business. It gives no guarantee of growth, competition law still applies, and the business must still follow listeners' tastes.

questions.stem: A merger between the two largest building supply chains in Queensland is reviewed by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission. The ACCC's main concern is likely to be whether the merger:
options: would allow the business to sell products online
would substantially lessen competition in the market
would change the name and logo of the merged business
would require the business to hire more apprentices
questions.explanation: The ACCC assesses whether a merger is likely to substantially lessen competition, for example by leaving customers with few alternatives. Branding, hiring and online sales are business decisions, not the ACCC's competition test.

questions.stem: Corporate social responsibility (CSR) means that a business:
options: considers the effects of its decisions on society and the environment
aims only to maximise the profit for its owners within the next year
is legally required to donate a share of its profit to charity
avoids all contact with customers, suppliers and the community
questions.explanation: CSR is a business's voluntary commitment to act in ways that benefit society and the environment beyond what the law requires. It is not a legal donation requirement or a focus on short-term profit alone.

questions.stem: A declining Queensland clothing brand repositions itself around recycled fabrics, a garment take-back scheme and published supplier audits. What is the relationship between sustainability, CSR and its strategy?
options: sustainability and CSR are unrelated to the brand's marketing or sales
the audits are required by law, so they cannot be part of its strategy
sustainable practices always cut costs, so its profit is guaranteed to rise
sustainable practices show CSR and give the brand a new point of difference
questions.explanation: Sustainable, responsible practices can be the basis of a repositioning that appeals to environmentally aware customers. Such practices often raise costs, and they go beyond legal requirements.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a business applying high ethical standards while repositioning in decline?
options: telling staff honestly and early about planned job losses and support
keeping planned job losses secret until the day staff are dismissed
advertising old stock as 'new' to clear it before closing a product line
cutting safety training to save money while sales continue to fall
questions.explanation: Honest, early communication about redundancies treats staff fairly and maintains trust. Hiding job losses, misleading advertising and cutting safety training are unethical, and some may also be unlawful.

questions.stem: Crisis management is:
options: the process of recruiting senior managers from outside the business
planning and responding to an event that threatens the business's reputation
the routine management of a business's inventory levels and production schedule
a strategy for setting a high launch price and lowering it over time
questions.explanation: Crisis management prepares for and responds to unexpected events, such as product recalls or data breaches, that threaten a business. Public relations is a key part of the response.

questions.stem: A Gold Coast food manufacturer discovers some of its products may be contaminated. Which response best shows the relationship between public relations and ethical practice?
options: blame its supplier in the media before any investigation has taken place
issue a statement that there is no problem while it investigates in private
recall the products quickly, tell the public openly and explain what is being fixed
say nothing publicly and quietly replace the stock to protect short-term sales
questions.explanation: Acting quickly and transparently protects consumers, which is ethical, and also protects long-term reputation, which is the goal of public relations. Hiding or denying a problem risks harm to customers and a much bigger loss of trust.

questions.stem: A business in decline sells an unused warehouse and uses the cash to repay debt. Which key business function strategy is this?
options: an operations strategy to raise the quality of its products
a financial strategy to improve liquidity and reduce debt
a marketing strategy to reposition the brand for customers
a human resources strategy to retrain and redeploy its staff
questions.explanation: Selling surplus assets and repaying debt is a financial management strategy that improves the business's cash position and solvency. It does not directly change marketing, staffing or product quality.

questions.stem: A business in steady state targets a new segment by redesigning its product, changing its promotion and moving to online channels. This is mainly a strategy of which key business function?
options: accounting
marketing
finance
human resources
questions.explanation: Changing the product, promotion and distribution to reach a new segment is a marketing strategy. Finance, human resources and operations would support it, but the strategy itself is marketing.

questions.stem: Redundancy occurs when:
options: an employee chooses to resign to take up another job
an employee is dismissed for serious misconduct at work
an employee reaches retirement age and decides to leave
an employee's job is no longer needed by the business
questions.explanation: Redundancy is when a business no longer needs a job to be done, for example because of new technology or falling demand. Resignation and retirement are the employee's choice, and dismissal follows misconduct or poor performance.

questions.stem: A Mackay sugar processor automates its packing line. Rather than make the packing staff redundant, it trains them to operate and maintain the new machines. This shows the relationship between:
options: Porter's five forces and rebranding through a change of company name
operations strategy and human resources strategy through retraining
marketing strategy and financial strategy through a new price list
exit strategy and crisis management through voluntary administration
questions.explanation: The operations change (automation) is matched by a human resources response (retraining), keeping skilled, loyal staff. Retraining can avoid redundancy costs and keep the knowledge staff already have.

questions.stem: A business in decline must cut labour costs by 20%. Which approach best balances efficiency with stakeholder satisfaction?
options: stop paying superannuation for a year so no staff need to leave
offer voluntary redundancies and retraining before any forced redundancies
make 20% of staff redundant at once with no notice given or support offered
cut every employee's pay below the award to avoid any redundancies
questions.explanation: Voluntary redundancy and retraining reduce costs while treating staff fairly, protecting morale and reputation. Paying below the award or stopping superannuation is unlawful, and sudden cuts without support damage trust.

questions.stem: A declining video rental chain repositions as a streaming and gaming service using cloud technology and data analytics. Which statement best describes the role of emerging technology here?
options: it affects only the finance function, as cloud services lower the taxes it pays
it has no link to the business's decline, as technology is unrelated
it removes the need for the business to understand its customers' needs
it changes the product, operations and marketing of the business together
questions.explanation: Emerging technology reshapes what the business sells, how it delivers it and how it reaches customers, linking several key business functions. Technology was likely a cause of the decline, so it is closely related.

questions.stem: Which list gives Porter's five forces?
options: supplier power, buyer power, competitive rivalry, threat of substitution, threat of entry
strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, threats and competitive rivalry in the market
sociocultural, technological, economic, environmental and political factors
lower cost, differentiation, cost focus, differentiation focus and innovation
questions.explanation: Porter's five forces analyse the competitive pressures in an industry. The other lists mix up SWOT, STEEPLE and Porter's separate generic strategies.

questions.stem: A Queensland supermarket chain buys most of the output of a small dairy, which has no other large customers. In a five forces analysis of the dairy, this means:
options: rivalry is very low
buyer power is high
supplier power is high
threat of entry is high
questions.explanation: When one customer buys most of a supplier's output, that buyer can push prices down, so buyer power is high. Supplier power describes the strength of the dairy's own suppliers.

questions.stem: Video calling software has reduced demand for business air travel. In Porter's five forces, for an airline this is:
options: buyer power
the threat of substitution
the threat of new entrants
supplier power
questions.explanation: A substitute is a different product that meets the same need, here holding a meeting without travelling. The threat of entry would be new airlines entering the market.

questions.stem: Which situation shows a low threat of entry into an industry?
options: there are many small firms selling products that are almost identical
starting up requires huge capital investment and government licences
a new business can start trading cheaply from home with a website
customers can switch suppliers easily at almost no cost to them
questions.explanation: High start-up costs and licensing are barriers to entry, which keep new rivals out. Cheap, easy start-up means a high threat of entry, and easy switching or many similar firms describe buyer power and rivalry.

questions.stem: A business relies on the only supplier in Australia of a specialised component, and no substitute component exists. In a five forces analysis, this means:
options: the threat of substitution is high for the business's product
competitive rivalry is high among the component's suppliers
supplier power is high, so the supplier can raise prices
buyer power is high, so the business can demand discounts
questions.explanation: A single supplier of an essential input with no substitutes has strong bargaining power over its customers. There is no rivalry among suppliers when only one exists.

questions.stem: A five forces analysis of a Brisbane taxi company shows high rivalry from rideshare firms, a high threat of substitution and high buyer power from app-based price comparison. What is the most valid implication for repositioning?
options: the industry is unattractive, so the business needs a clear point of difference
the industry is highly attractive, so the business should raise its fares
only supplier power matters, so the business should change its fuel supplier
the forces cancel each other out, so no change in strategy is required
questions.explanation: Several strong forces reduce profitability, so the business must differentiate, for example through service, safety or niche markets, or consider other options. Raising fares when buyers have strong power and substitutes would likely lose customers.

questions.stem: A declining coal-fired electricity business in Queensland considers repositioning into solar and battery storage. A STEEPLE analysis shows falling battery costs, government renewable energy targets and growing community concern about emissions. These factors are, in order:
options: legal, technological and economic, with only the first supporting it
technological, political and sociocultural, all supporting the repositioning
economic, legal and ethical, all working against the repositioning
environmental, sociocultural and technological, all working against the move
questions.explanation: Falling battery costs are technological, government targets are political, and community concern is sociocultural; all three favour a move to renewables. Misclassifying the factors leads to the wrong conclusion about their direction.

questions.stem: The owners of a declining Rockhampton furniture store compare two options using business criteria: (1) close and sell the stock and fittings; (2) reposition as an online seller of locally made furniture. Which statement best evaluates the options?
options: both options rate equally on every criterion, as neither one would affect any stakeholder
option 2 may restore competitiveness but carries more risk; option 1 is certain but ends the business
option 1 rates highest on competitiveness because closing removes every rival from the market
option 2 cannot be evaluated, as business criteria apply only to businesses in the growth stage
questions.explanation: Business criteria weigh competitiveness, effectiveness, efficiency and stakeholder satisfaction, so the repositioning offers a chance of renewed competitiveness at greater risk, while closing is certain but ends jobs and the business. Business criteria apply at every stage of the life cycle.

questions.stem: A sole trader's florist shop is in decline and its debts exceed its assets. Why is this situation especially serious for the owner?
options: a sole trader must enter voluntary administration under company law immediately
the owner's debts are automatically paid by the government once the shop closes
a sole trader cannot sell the business, as only companies can be sold to buyers
unlimited liability means the owner's personal assets can be used to pay the debts
questions.explanation: A sole trader is not a separate legal entity, so the owner is personally liable for all business debts. Voluntary administration is a process for companies, and sole traders can sell their businesses.

questions.stem: A business in steady state invests in leadership and digital skills courses for its existing managers so they can lead a planned repositioning. This is best described as:
options: staff development that builds the capability needed for the new strategy
a redundancy program that reduces the number of managers in the business
an involuntary exit forced on the business by its creditors and the court
a rebrand that changes the business's logo and slogan for its customers
questions.explanation: Development builds employees' skills for future roles, which supports repositioning. It keeps staff rather than removing them, and it does not change the business's visual identity.
